title: Conjecture on r-free digraphs with r > 2n/3
statement_text: All $r$-free digraphs on $n$ vertices with $r > 2n/3$ are at most one edge away from being acyclic.
context_text: For a digraph $G$, a feedback arc set is a set of edges whose deletion leaves an acyclic digraph, and $\beta(G)$ is the minimum size of a feedback arc set. Ordering the vertices arbitrarily and deleting the smaller of the sets of forward and backward edges shows $\beta(G)\le m/2$ for any oriented graph with $m$ edges, and by Berger and Shor $\beta(G)\le m/2-\Omega(m^{3/4})$ always; the quantity $m/2-\beta(G)$ is called the directed surplus. A digraph is $r$-free if it contains no directed cycle of length at most $r$; "at most one edge away from being acyclic" means $\beta(G)\le1$. Previous work bounded $\beta(G)$ for $r$-free digraphs in terms of the number of non-adjacent pairs (Chudnovsky–Seymour–Sullivan, Sullivan, and Fox–Keevash–Sudakov, who proved $\beta(G)\le 800\gamma(G)/r^2$ where $\gamma(G)$ is the number of non-adjacent unordered pairs of vertices). The authors construct $r$-free digraphs $G$ on $n$ vertices with $\beta(G)\ge n^2/(r+1)^2$, so if every $r$-free digraph on $n$ vertices has $\beta(G)=O(1)$ then $r=\Omega(n)$. In the converse direction they pose this conjecture, and note it would be tight: for $n$ a multiple of $3$ there is an $(r-1)$-free digraph on $n$ vertices with $r=2n/3$ and $\beta(G)=2$.

title: Suspected directed surplus of a random B-free orientation (Remark 1.6)
statement_text: A random orientation of a $\mathcal{B}$-free undirected graph on $n$ vertices with $m = \mathrm{ex}(n, \mathcal{B})$ edges likely satisfies $\beta(G) = m/2 - \Omega(\sqrt{mn})$.
context_text: For a digraph $G$, a feedback arc set is a set of edges whose deletion leaves an acyclic digraph, and $\beta(G)$ is the minimum size of a feedback arc set. Ordering the vertices arbitrarily and deleting the smaller of the sets of forward and backward edges shows $\beta(G)\le m/2$ for any oriented graph with $m$ edges, and by Berger and Shor $\beta(G)\le m/2-\Omega(m^{3/4})$ always; the quantity $m/2-\beta(G)$ is called the directed surplus. For a family $\mathcal{B}$ of undirected graphs, a graph is $\mathcal{B}$-free if it contains no member of $\mathcal{B}$ as a subgraph, and the extremal number $\mathrm{ex}(n,\mathcal{B})$ is the maximum number of edges of a $\mathcal{B}$-free graph on $n$ vertices. The authors prove that if $\mathrm{ex}(n,\mathcal{B})=O(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ then every digraph $G$ with $m$ edges whose underlying undirected graph is $\mathcal{B}$-free has $\beta(G)\le m/2-c\,m^{3/4+\varepsilon/(4(2-\varepsilon))}$, and that this is tight up to the constant when $\mathrm{ex}(n,\mathcal{B})=\Theta(n^{2-\varepsilon})$: a random orientation $G$ of an extremal $\mathcal{B}$-free graph on $n$ vertices with $m=\mathrm{ex}(n,\mathcal{B})$ edges satisfies $\beta(G)\ge m/2-C\,m^{3/4+\varepsilon/(4(2-\varepsilon))}$, which for such $m$ equals $m/2-O(\sqrt{mn})$. They remark that the condition $\mathrm{ex}(n,\mathcal{B})=\Theta(n^{2-\varepsilon})$ is used only for convenience (the proof works under some mild conditions on $\mathrm{ex}(n,\mathcal{B})$), and suspect that in general such a random orientation satisfies $\beta(G)=m/2-\Omega(\sqrt{mn})$ (as written in the paper; since the remark is about the proof of the lower bound on $\beta(G)$, the intended meaning may be that the directed surplus of the random orientation is of order $\sqrt{mn}$).
